run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_223 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Both requested items were checked against the configured SQL Server (database testdb, target m0-otel-20260909). (1) The database contains exactly two tables, dbo.holmes_eval_223 and dbo.orders. The single row in dbo.holmes_eval_223 (id=1, category eval_test) carries verification_code HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9. (2) dbo.orders has 10,000 rows across 1,000 distinct customer_id values (1..1000) and only one index, the clustered primary key on id; there is no index on customer_id. A probe query with the same predicate (WHERE customer_id = 12345) was planned as a Clustered Index Scan with 64 logical reads and no index seek, and SQL Server's missing-index DMV itself records [customer_id] as an equality column with avg_user_impact 93.98 for [testdb].[dbo].[orders]. That is the mechanism that makes this query scale linearly with table size; it is a hypothesis about the reported slowness, not an observed slow execution, because no cached entry for the exact statement SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 exists in sys.dm_exec_query_stats and the equivalent probe cost only ~782 us at the current 10,000-row size. Also notable: the literal 12345 is outside the actual customer_id domain (1..1000) and returns 0 rows, so the statement may be a bad-parameter bug rather than a genuinely expensive query.

claims.text: Database testdb contains exactly two tables: dbo.holmes_eval_223 and dbo.orders.
dbo.holmes_eval_223 has columns id (int, PK), category (nvarchar), verification_code (nvarchar), created_at (datetime); its only index is the primary key on id.
The row in dbo.holmes_eval_223 is id=1, category='eval_test', verification_code='HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9', created_at=2026-11-23T18:43:32.540.

dbo.orders has five columns (id int, customer_id int, order_date date, total_amount decimal, status nvarchar) and only one index: the clustered primary key PK__orders__3213E83F14CB338B on id; there is no nonclustered index on customer_id.
dbo.orders currently holds 10,000 rows with 1,000 distinct customer_id values, and customer_id ranges from 1 to 1000.
The literal 12345 matches no rows: SELECT COUNT(*) ... FROM dbo.orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 returned rows_for_customer = 0 with NULL first_order/last_order.

For the predicate customer_id = 12345 the cached plan contains a Clustered Index Scan and no index seek; that probe execution read 64 logical pages and averaged 782 us elapsed / 782 us CPU per execution.
Index usage statistics for dbo.orders show only PK__orders__3213E83F14CB338B with user_seeks = 0, user_scans = 3 and user_updates = 10,000 since the counters were last reset.

SQL Server's own missing-index DMV reports for [testdb].[dbo].[orders] an equality column [customer_id] with avg_user_impact 93.98, avg_total_user_cost 0.0643 and user_seeks 1 (no included columns suggested).

At the current data size the scan is cheap in absolute terms: a comparable customer_id-filtered aggregate read 64 logical pages and averaged 782 us elapsed, so the missing index is a scalability risk rather than a demonstrated cause of large latency now; no measured slow execution of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 was observed.

The primary candidate cause of the reported slowness is the absence of a nonclustered index on dbo.orders.customer_id: every execution must scan the full clustered index (64 pages / 10,000 rows today) instead of seeking ~10 matching rows, and that cost grows linearly with table growth.

A second candidate, not verified: the literal 12345 lies outside the actual customer_id domain (1..1000), so the statement inevitably scans and returns nothing; if the application passes such ids regularly, the observed 'slowness' may be a wrong-parameter/expectation problem rather than an expensive plan.

Further candidate causes left open because no wait, blocking, client-timing or network data was available: SELECT * pulling all five columns (including decimal total_amount) fattening the result/network payload, parameter sniffing on a cached plan, and lock waits from the 10,000 row updates recorded on the table.
A heap / missing-primary-key layout is not the cause: dbo.orders has a clustered primary key on id and shows clustered-index scan (not heap) plans.

Support the predicate with an index targgeted at this query, e.g. CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_orders_customer_id ON dbo.orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (order_date, total_amount, status); the INCLUDE set makes SELECT * covering for the current five columns and avoids key lookups.
Validate the parameter before blaming the plan: confirm which customer_id values the application actually sends, since 12345 cannot match rows in a table whose customer_id spans 1..1000.

Replace SELECT * with the explicit column list the caller needs, and capture a live actual execution plan with SET STATISTICS IO, TIME plus wait/blocking data from an authorized operator session before concluding the query is genuinely slow.

gaps: No measured latency history exists for the exact statement 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345': filtering sys.dm_exec_query_stats on '%customer_id%' returned only the 10,000-iteration insert loop and the two probe queries I ran, so the claim that this query is slow is not independently verified.
The plan and read-count evidence comes from an equivalent probe query (COUNT/MIN/MAX with WHERE customer_id = 12345), not from the exact SELECT * statement.

No wait statistics, blocking/lock-wait data, client-side timing, network or server resource metrics were available, so parameter sniffing, blocking and payload/network cost remain unchecked rather than excluded.
The physical size query on sys.partitions failed (SQL_INVALID, error 207: invalid column name 'used_page_count'), so table page counts beyond the 64 logical reads observed are unknown.
The change_history integration is not configured in this Run, so any recent index/schema or configuration change to dbo.orders cannot be checked.
next_steps: Have a DBA capture the actual execution plan and SET STATISTICS IO/TIME for the real statement from the application, and compare logical reads before and after adding the (customer_id) index.
Check sys.dm_os_wait_stats, sys.dm_exec_requests and blocking chains during a slow execution to rule in or out lock waits and parameter sniffing.
Confirm with the application owner which customer_id range is valid (1..1000 per current data) so the query parameter is not silently out of domain.
